title: Signs you can touch
hook: Catholics and Orthodox count seven sacraments; most Protestants two ordinances; Quakers keep them inwardly

segments.voice: Yesterday: your story in three sentences, a testimony. Your line was your story counts. Now a new week, and the last of this camp: the sacraments, briefly.
screen: `YOUR STORY COUNTS.` → `A NEW WEEK: THE SACRAMENTS.`

segments.voice: A ring slid onto a finger. A hand on a shoulder at a funeral. A handshake that closes a deal. A hug at the airport. None of them needs a word. People are bodies, and the deepest things they mean, they tend to say with hands, with objects, with water and bread and touch. Christianity is full of this. Water poured over a baby's head. Bread broken and shared. Oil smoothed on a sick person's forehead. Hands laid on someone being sent out. For many Christians these are not just symbols. They're where God meets people, through ordinary stuff. And the churches count them differently.
screen: `A RING, A HANDSHAKE, A HUG.` → `WATER, BREAD, OIL, HANDS.` → `WHERE GOD MEETS PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Sacrament comes from the Latin sacramentum, and before the church used it, it meant a soldier's oath of loyalty, something sacred that binds you. Early Latin Christians used it to translate a Greek word, mysterion, mystery; Orthodox Christians still call the sacraments the holy mysteries. A classic definition, from the Anglican Book of Common Prayer: a sacrament is "an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace." Outward and visible: water, bread, wine, oil. Inward and spiritual: what God gives through them. The churches count differently. Catholics count seven, and Orthodox Christians usually name the same seven: baptism; confirmation, which Orthodox call chrismation; the Eucharist; confession; anointing of the sick; marriage; and ordination. Most Protestant churches name two, baptism and the Lord's Supper, because Jesus commanded those two directly. Many Baptists and others prefer the word ordinance: something ordered by Christ, done in obedience and remembrance. Anglicans and Lutherans hold the two as sacraments and treat the others as sacred rites. A few, like Quakers and the Salvation Army, keep no outward sacraments at all. Not because they don't care, but because they believe the reality should be lived inwardly and in every ordinary moment, not in a few set rites. Churches disagree about this in earnest, and each has reasons. What they share is the conviction that God isn't only up in the clouds. God comes close through water on skin, bread in a hand, a word spoken over you. Grace, for many Christians, comes wrapped in the most ordinary things.
screen: `SACRAMENTUM — A SACRED OATH.` · `OUTWARD SIGN, INWARD GRACE.` · `SEVEN, TWO, OR NONE OUTWARDLY.` · `GOD COMES CLOSE THROUGH ORDINARY THINGS.` · then, large: `AN OUTWARD AND VISIBLE SIGN.`

segments.voice: Think of the ordinary things you'll touch today: water from the tap or in a glass, bread or whatever your bread is, lotion or oil on your hands, the hand of someone you love. Pick one and imagine it carrying more than it seems to: care, welcome, life. If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, just let it be more than ordinary for a minute.
Sacrament. From the Latin for a sacred oath. An outward sign of inward grace: water, bread, oil, hands.
Your line: grace comes in ordinary things. Water, bread, oil, hands. That's day one hundred fifty-one.

chat.says: Why do some churches have seven sacraments and others only two?
options: Catholics and Orthodox count seven; most Protestants name two that Jesus directly commanded.
It depends on the country: each nation's church simply picked its own number.
Churches with two just shortened the list to keep their services quicker.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think about'; Orthodox count softened to 'usually name the same seven' (Orthodox do not always fix the number); dated 'Middle Ages' claim cut from the trapdoor.
BCP 1662 Catechism: 'an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace given unto us'. Confirm exact wording.

The seven named for Catholic and Orthodox: baptism, confirmation/chrismation, Eucharist, penance/confession, anointing of the sick/holy unction, matrimony, holy orders. Orthodox do not always fix the number at seven; confirm phrasing 'count seven'.
Anglican (Article 25) and Lutheran positions simplified to 'two sacraments, the others sacred rites'. Confirm.
Quakers and the Salvation Army: no outward sacraments. Confirm description.
Trapdoor: Tertullian's use of sacramentum; the seven fixed by Peter Lombard (12th c.) and confirmed at councils (Lyon 1274, Florence 1439, Trent). Confirm 'in the Middle Ages'.
